title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
summary: Learn to choose the chart type that best makes a specific stakeholder point, and to simplify a chart by removing clutter that adds visual effort without adding information.

steps.title: The Chart Must Match the Point
steps.lede: During your own exploration you might have built a bar chart, a line plot, and a box plot of the delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which one actually makes the Lagos point?

blocks.text: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories — showing average delivery time side by side across Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time — showing Lagos delivery time rising from Month 1 to Month 2. A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship and is best used to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%). Chart choice is driven by the point you are making, not by the data alone.

steps.title: Why the Chart Type Must Match the Point
steps.lede: Watch how the same data looks different depending on chart type, and notice when a chart makes comparison easy versus hard.

segments.label: Bar chart vs. pie chart: comparing values across categories
segments.summary: The same time-use data (sleep, work, eat, rest) is shown first as a pie chart, then as a bar chart. The pie makes it hard to judge which slice is larger when two slices are close in size. The bar chart, with its common baseline, makes the one-hour difference between working and sleeping immediately readable. A second example pits two pie charts against a grouped bar chart to answer 'does Earl work more than Herman, and by how much?' — a question the pies struggle to answer and the bar chart resolves at a glance.

segments.label: Boxplots: strong for distributions, but risky with unfamiliar audiences
segments.summary: A boxplot is considered as a candidate for showing distributions across multiple groups. Two practical problems emerge: sparse data on some days would produce boxes with no box body, and — more broadly — boxplots are not a widely recognised chart type, so an audience unfamiliar with them faces a steeper learning curve. The presenter notes that a specialist audience (researchers and physicians) may be the exception, but still sets the boxplot aside in favour of continuing to explore other options.

steps.title: Pie Charts, Scatterplots, and a Common Misconception
steps.lede: Two more chart types worth knowing — and one trap to avoid.

blocks.text: A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship: if the point is 'Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume,' a pie chart of each city's share of total orders fits that framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not. The pie must depict a meaningful whole — values that sum to 100%.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience — useful to keep in mind if the distance/delivery-time relationship ever needs to go in front of the manager directly.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths, since both show a value at a glance — but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye.

steps.title: Scatterplot: Exploratory or Communicative?
steps.lede: A scatterplot of distance_km vs delivery_minutes is shown. Is this chart primarily exploratory or communicative?

public.prompt: A scatterplot of distance_km vs delivery_minutes is shown. Is this chart primarily exploratory or communicative?

options.text: Exploratory — scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it
Communicative — scatterplots are designed to present findings to stakeholders
Both — scatterplots work equally well for exploration and communication
Neither — scatterplots are only used for statistical modeling

opt_exploratory.message: Correct. A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For stakeholder communication, you would typically choose a simpler chart type.

opt_communicative.message: Not quite. Scatterplots are powerful for exploration, but they are often too complex for stakeholder communication. Simpler chart types like bar charts or line graphs are usually better for presenting findings.

opt_both.message: Not quite. While scatterplots can be used for both purposes, they are primarily exploratory tools. For communication, simpler chart types are usually more effective.

opt_neither.message: Not quite. Scatterplots are used for exploration and can support modeling, but their primary role is to help analysts understand relationships in the data.

correct.message: Right. Scatterplots are exploratory tools. For stakeholder communication, choose simpler chart types that match your point.

incorrect.message: Remember: scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For stakeholders, simpler charts are usually better.

hints: Think about whether a scatterplot is easy for a non-technical audience to interpret.
Scatterplots show many individual data points — is that level of detail needed for communication?

steps.title: Remove the Clutter, Keep the Data
steps.lede: A bar chart built during your own exploration can carry gridlines, a border, and precise decimal labels that help you double-check the numbers. The operations manager probably doesn't need any of that to get the point.

blocks.text: Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point directly instead of relying on gridlines. A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value — white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border. Data labels should be used sparingly, only where exact values are important; otherwise remove them and use the axis instead.

Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels — '22.00 minutes' becomes '22 min'. Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally instead. City names as short as Lagos, Abuja, and Kano do not need to be rotated at all.

steps.title: Simplifying a Chart Step by Step
steps.lede: Watch each removal reduce reading effort. The presenter uses Excel; the same design principles apply in any charting tool.

segments.label: Removing chart clutter: border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, and excess data labels
segments.summary: The presenter opens by explaining that every chart element adds cognitive burden, and that overwhelming an audience risks losing them entirely — establishing why decluttering matters. Working on a bar chart in Excel, they remove the chart border (noting white space does the job of separation better), delete the gridlines and shaded background, then reformat the y-axis to drop trailing zeros by switching to thousands units with a 'k' suffix. They then abbreviate the diagonal month labels on the x-axis to horizontal text, citing research that diagonal text takes fifty percent longer to read. Finally, they weigh whether exact values are needed: deciding they are not, they delete all data labels and keep the y-axis instead, leaving a much cleaner chart.

steps.title: Identifying Clutter to Remove
steps.lede: Which elements should be removed from a bar chart prepared for a non-technical operations manager?

public.prompt: Which elements should be removed from a bar chart prepared for a non-technical operations manager?

options.text: Gridlines and the chart border, since they add no informative value
Axis labels, since the bars speak for themselves
All data labels, since they clutter the chart
Nothing — all elements are necessary for clarity

opt_gridlines_border.message: Correct. Gridlines can be deleted if precise values are not critical, and a chart's border can be removed since it adds no informative value. White space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content.

opt_axis_labels.message: Not quite. Axis labels are essential for understanding what the chart shows. Removing them would make the chart confusing, not simpler.

opt_data_labels.message: Not quite. Data labels should be used sparingly, but they are helpful where exact values matter. The goal is to remove elements that add no informative value, not all labels.

opt_nothing.message: Not quite. Many chart elements add clutter without adding information. Gridlines and borders can often be removed to let the audience focus on the data.

correct.message: Right. Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be taken, rather than decoding the chart.

incorrect.message: Think about which elements add informative value and which are just decoration. Gridlines and borders often fall into the decoration category.

hints: Which elements help the audience understand the data, and which are just visual decoration?
Gridlines and borders can often be removed without losing clarity.

steps.title: Why Remove the Border?
steps.lede: What does removing a chart's border achieve?

public.prompt: What does removing a chart's border achieve?

options.text: It reduces clutter; white space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content
It makes the chart look more modern and professional
It makes the chart area larger so more data can be shown
Nothing — borders are necessary to define the chart boundaries

opt_white_space.message: Correct. A chart's border can be removed since it is not adding informative value; white space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content.

opt_modern.message: Not quite. While removing borders may look modern, the real benefit is reducing clutter. The border adds no informative value, and white space is sufficient for separation.

opt_larger.message: Not quite. Removing the border does not significantly increase the chart area. The benefit is reducing clutter by removing an element that adds no informative value.

opt_nothing.message: Not quite. Borders are not necessary to define chart boundaries. White space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content, and removing the border reduces clutter.

correct.message: Exactly. Borders add no informative value. White space is sufficient to separate the chart from surrounding content.

incorrect.message: Think about whether the border adds information or just decoration. White space can do the job of separating the chart.

hints: Does the border tell the audience anything about the data?
White space can separate the chart from surrounding content without needing a border.

steps.title: Simplify the Delivery-Time Chart
steps.lede: A bar chart of city delivery times is shown with a border, gridlines, trailing-zero axis labels, rotated city-name tick labels, and data labels on every bar. Apply the simplification principles to clean it up for the operations manager.

public.instruction:
A chart showing delivery times by city has gridlines, a border, trailing zeros in axis labels (e.g., '40.0'), and rotated city-name labels. Edit the chart to simplify it for a non-technical audience by:
• Removing the gridlines
• Removing the border
• Removing trailing zeros from axis labels (e.g., change '40.0' to '40')
• Making city-name labels horizontal (not rotated)
• Removing per-bar data labels if present

Do not change the underlying delivery-time values.
checklist: Trailing zeros removed from axis labels

rubric.criterion: Gridlines have been removed from the chart
Trailing zeros have been removed from axis labels (e.g., '40.0' → '40')
City-name tick labels are horizontal (not rotated)
Per-bar data labels have been removed
The underlying delivery-time values are unchanged

correct.message: Excellent. You've successfully simplified the chart by removing clutter (gridlines, border, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and data labels) while preserving the underlying data.

incorrect.message: Review the simplification checklist: remove gridlines, border, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and per-bar data labels. Keep the underlying delivery-time values unchanged.

hints: Gridlines and borders add visual clutter without informative value.
Trailing zeros (like '.0') can be removed from axis labels.
Horizontal labels are easier to read than rotated ones.
Data labels should be removed unless the exact values are critical to the audience.

steps.title: Chart Matching and Simplifying — Key Takeaways
steps.lede: What you practised in this tile.

blocks.text: Match the chart type to the stakeholder point: bar for category comparison, line for change over time, pie for part-to-whole, scatterplot for relationships. Reduce clutter before presenting: remove borders, gridlines, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and unnecessary data labels. Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.

remediation_steps.title: Scatterplots: Exploration vs. Communication
remediation_steps.lede: A scatterplot of distance_km vs delivery_minutes helps you understand the data — but is it the right chart to show the operations manager?

blocks.text: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. It shows the relationship between two numerical variables — distance and delivery time — which is useful when you are exploring whether a pattern exists. When communicating to a stakeholder, a bar chart or line chart usually makes the point more directly, because the audience can read it without needing to interpret a cloud of dots. The scatterplot stays in your exploratory toolkit; the bar or line chart goes in the presentation.
